title: `eventBridgeServerPixelUpdate` and `pubSubServerPixelUpdate` now require user access to the app
summary:
Starting November 20, 2026, the eventBridgeServerPixelUpdate and pubSubServerPixelUpdate mutations reject online access tokens for users who don't have access to the app. The change applies to all GraphQL Admin API versions.

What changed

Both mutations now require an offline access token, or an online access token for a user who has access to the app. The write_pixels, read_customer_events, and write_server_pixels access scope requirements don't change.

When the check fails, the mutation returns an access denied error and no payload, and the server pixel's endpoint stays the same. The error message is the same one you get for a missing access scope, so it doesn't mention user access.

Who's affected

This affects apps that call these mutations with an online access token for a staff member who doesn't have access to the app. Offline access tokens, and online access tokens for users who have access to the app, work as before.

If your app calls these mutations with online access tokens, then make sure the staff member has access to your app in the Shopify admin, or call the mutations with an offline access token, for example from a background job. Handle the access denied error either way.

Why this matters

The update mutations now make the same user access check that serverPixelCreate and serverPixelDelete already make, so only a user who has access to an app can change where its server pixel sends events. This is a security fix, so it applies to all API versions without a deprecation period.

title: App security updates: IP allowlist due tomorrow
summary:
The busiest shopping weeks of the year are almost here. Thanks to everyone who’s already turned on an IP allowlist, enabled expiring tokens, and taken other steps to help keep merchants protected when it matters most.

This Friday, November 20, is the deadline for IP allowlist. We’re also sharing requirements that start December 1, and tooling updates to help you get ready for the next round of security improvements.

Action required

  • Public apps without an IP allowlist are delisted after November 20, 2026 Enable IP allowlists now to avoid delisting and being blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working but will be flagged in merchant Settings > Apps if they’re not compliant. Your app will be relisted automatically when you add an IP allowlist. Don’t wait, it only takes a few minutes. Read the dev docs to learn how.
  • Custom apps need IP allowlist before being installed. After November 20, 2026, an IP allowlist must be enabled on a custom app before installing it on a store outside your organization. Read the changelog
  • Network access declarations required for apps that run on the online store. Apps that run code on the online store must declare allowed_sources in the network_access section of shopify.app.toml. The first deadline is December 1, 2026, followed by January 1, 2027. Read the changelog
  • Expiring offline access tokens will be required for every custom app created on or after December 1, 2026. Read the changelog
  • Apps that read abandoned checkout recovery URLs will require level 2 protected customer data access starting December 1, 2026 for public apps and January 1, 2027 for partner custom apps. If your app uses these URLs, request access to name, email, phone, and address before your deadline. Read the changelog
  • Merchant custom apps need to enable bulk operations before use. Merchant custom apps created in the Dev Dashboard or the Shopify admin must now explicitly enable bulk queries and mutations within the Settings section of the Dev Dashboard. Read the dev docs
  • Multi-factor authentication is now required on every partner account. Turn it on now; we recommend passkeys.

For other upcoming security deadlines, see the security deadlines calendar.

Also new this week

  • Admin-created custom apps are now in Dev Dashboard, giving them the same high quality security tools as all other apps, including IP allowlists, API logs, and expiring tokens. Existing tokens keep working. Read the changelog
  • Declare that your app uses only expiring access tokens. Turn on the Admin API token expiry card in your app’s Settings to reject requests for non-expiring tokens, giving you confidence your migration is complete ahead of the deadline. Read the changelog

Get help

If you see something suspicious, tell us right away at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You're responsible for fixing it and notifying affected merchants, and we'll support you through it. For general security questions, contact Shopify Support.

For guidance on all our security practices, and a complete timeline, see the App Security Hub. We're here to answer questions on the App Security board in the developer community.

title: Show image swatches for product options in the Catalog API
summary:
The Catalog API can now return an image for each product option value, such as a color, so you can show buyers a picture of each choice instead of only its name. Swatches are available when you request full product details with get_product. The new field is optional, and existing integrations keep working without changes.

What changed

In a get_product response, an option value can include a swatch object. Each swatch has one field, image_url, which is the URL of an image that represents the option value. Not every option value has a swatch. When a value has no swatch data, the response omits swatch.

search_catalog and lookup_catalog don’t return swatches, and swatches aren’t part of a variant’s options array. You don’t need to change your agent profile to get them.

Who’s affected

You’re affected if your app or agent calls get_product and shows product options to buyers, for example in a variant picker on a product page. If you only call search_catalog or lookup_catalog, nothing changes.

What to do

No action is required. If you don’t read swatch, your integration keeps working as before.

To show swatches:

  1. Read product.options[].values[].swatch.image_url from the get_product response.
  2. Show the image beside the option value or in its place, and keep the label visible or available to screen readers.
  3. When a value has no swatch, or its image doesn’t load, show the label.
  4. Use available and exists to set each option’s state. Don’t treat a missing swatch as an unavailable option.

Related docs

  • Option swatches in the Global Catalog extension reference
  • get_product in the Global Catalog MCP reference

title: Function settings extensions can now report several errors at once
summary:
Function settings extensions can now report several errors at once. When your s-function-settings onSubmit handler rejects with an AggregateError, the Shopify admin shows every error on discount and checkout rule pages instead of only one. No action is required.

What changed

Previously, the admin showed one error when your extension rejected the promise you passed to event.waitUntil() in onSubmit, using the message of that error.

Now you can reject with an AggregateError, and the admin shows the message of each entry in its errors list. Each entry is an Error, and you can give it a code string.

  • The admin shows up to 10 errors. Each message is trimmed to 300 characters, and duplicate messages appear once.
  • Your onError handler receives the same entries, with their codes, so you can mark the fields in your own UI.
  • An entry with no code, or a code that is empty or longer than 64 characters, gets a default code: UNKNOWN on discount pages and EXTENSION_ERROR on checkout rule pages.
  • Rejecting with a single Error still works and shows one error.

The onerror property of s-function-settings is now typed as the AggregateError it receives in @shopify/ui-extensions 2025-10, 2026-10, and the 2027-01 release candidate.

Who's affected

This applies to apps with a function settings extension on discount or checkout rule pages, built with Polaris web components on API version 2025-10 or later.

Extensions on earlier API versions keep the previous behavior and show a single message. Extensions that reject with a single Error also keep working as before.

Why this matters

When a merchant fills in several fields incorrectly, they now see every problem after one save. They do not have to fix one field, save, and then find the next error.

What to do

No action is required. To report several errors, reject with an AggregateError of Errors in your onSubmit handler:

function fieldError(code, message) {
  return Object.assign(new Error(message), {code});
}

async function save(settings) {
  const errors = [];
  if (!settings.minimumQuantity) {
    errors.push(fieldError('MINIMUM_QUANTITY_REQUIRED', 'Enter a minimum quantity.'));
  }
  if (settings.percentage > 100) {
    errors.push(fieldError('PERCENTAGE_TOO_HIGH', 'Percentage can be at most 100.'));
  }
  if (errors.length > 0) {
    throw new AggregateError(errors, 'Settings are not valid');
  }
  // apply your metafield changes here
}

 event.waitUntil(save(settings))}
  onError={(event) => {
    for (const error of event.error.errors) {
      console.log(error.code, error.message);
    }
  }}
>
  {/* your fields */}

This sample checks two fields and throws one AggregateError with an Error per invalid field. Replace the checks and codes with your own. To test your extension, save settings with several invalid fields on a development store and confirm that the admin lists each error.

Related docs

  • Discount Function Settings API reference
  • Build a discount UI extension with UI extensions

title: Network access declarations are now required for apps that run on the online store
summary:
We're adding network access declarations as a requirement to better protect merchants. Apps that run code on the online store must declare allowed_sources in the [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml.

Timeline

Shopify will reject deploys and delist apps that haven't added the required declarations as follows.

Public apps:

  • December 1, 2026: Shopify rejects deploys and Shopify App Store submissions. Merchants see a warning in the Shopify admin. Existing app versions keep working.
  • January 1, 2027: Shopify delists apps from the Shopify App Store and blocks new installs. Existing installs keep working.

Custom apps installed outside your organization:

  • December 1, 2026: Shopify rejects deploys.
  • January 1, 2027: Shopify blocks installs of your apps outside your organization until every app that's in scope declares its network access.

What apps are affected

Public apps, and custom apps that you install on stores outside your organization, are affected if they use any of the following features:

  • A theme app extension block or app embed.
  • Script tags on the online store.
  • An app proxy.
  • The write_themes access scope.
  • A web pixel with the write_open_pixels access scope.

What apps are unaffected

  • Apps that only write content, such as metafields, menus, or products.
  • Apps that have a checkout UI extension but none of the features listed above.
  • Custom apps that you install only on stores within your organization.
  • Apps that merchants create in the Dev Dashboard or in the Shopify admin.
  • Web pixels that run in the default strict sandbox.

Why we're making this change

Injected scripts can load code onto a storefront from any server. Declaring your app's servers helps Shopify spot suspicious requests, which protects your app and the merchants who use it.

What to do

  1. Add the servers that your app's code loads from or sends requests to, such as your API or CDN, to allowed_sources. If your app doesn't contact any external servers, then set allowed_sources = []. An empty list counts as a declaration.
  2. Optional: Add the hosts that your app links customers to, such as your app's own site, to allowed_navigation_hosts. This helps Shopify recognize links to sites that you trust, so customers are less likely to see an exit warning.
  3. Test your configuration on a dev store with the Network access testing preview. The preview covers the online store only.
  4. Run shopify app deploy, and then release the new version.

Here's an example configuration:

[network_access]
allowed_sources = ["https://api.app.example.com"]
allowed_navigation_hosts = ["app.example.com"]

For examples and troubleshooting, refer to Declare your app's network access. For every upcoming date, refer to Upcoming security deadlines.

title: Expiring offline access tokens required for new custom apps as of December 1, 2026
summary:
Starting December 1, 2026, every new custom app must request and use expiring offline access tokens for GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests. This has been required for new public apps since April 1, 2026. This update extends the requirement to new partner-created custom apps and merchant-created apps.

If you already request expiring offline tokens, you likely don’t need to change your app.

What changed

For apps created on or after December 1, 2026, Shopify requires expiring offline access tokens for Admin API calls:

  • New offline tokens that you obtain with the authorization code grant or token exchange must be expiring.
  • You request an expiring offline token by including expiring=1 in your token request and then storing and using the refresh token that Shopify returns.
  • Tokens that you obtain through the client credentials grant already expire after 24 hours, so this flow already meets the requirement.
  • Tokens that you obtain through application-only access already meet the requirement.

Existing custom apps and merchant-created apps that were set up before December 1, 2026 can keep using their existing offline tokens.

Who’s affected

The requirement for expiring offline access tokens applies to:

  • Custom apps created on or after December 1, 2026
  • Apps that merchants create on or after December 1, 2026

The following aren’t affected by this change:

  • Custom apps and merchant-created apps that were created before December 1, 2026
  • Public apps, which have already been required to use expiring offline tokens since April 1, 2026

Why this matters

Expiring offline access tokens limit how long a leaked token can be used. If an expiring token leaks, it stops working after a fixed amount of time unless your app refreshes it. A non-expiring token keeps working until the app is uninstalled or you rotate the app secret, which increases the risk from a leak.

What to do

  1. If your app uses token exchange or the authorization code grant:

    • Include expiring=1 in your token requests for offline access.
    • Store and use the refresh token that Shopify returns to obtain new access tokens when the current one expires.
    • If you use Shopify app templates or libraries, check that you’re on a recent version, because they already request expiring tokens by default.

  2. If your app uses the client credentials grant:

    • You don’t need to make any changes. Tokens from that grant already expire after 24 hours.

For setup details and examples, see the expiring offline access token guide in the Admin API docs: Use expiring offline access tokens.

title: Subscriptions now support store credit with `allowStoreCredit`
summary:
As of API version 2027-01, apps can read and manage store credit on subscriptions. When a customer opts in to store credit for an eligible subscription at checkout, Shopify applies the customer's store credit to each renewal first and charges the remaining balance to the saved payment method.

The change is available in the GraphQL Admin API and the Customer Account API. No action is required.

What changed

The GraphQL Admin API adds the following fields and inputs:

  • Selling plans: SellingPlanRecurringBillingPolicy.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit shows whether subscriptions on a selling plan can use store credit. You set it through paymentConfiguration on SellingPlanRecurringBillingPolicyInput, in sellingPlansToCreate and sellingPlansToUpdate on sellingPlanGroupCreate and sellingPlanGroupUpdate.
  • Contracts: SubscriptionContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit and SubscriptionBillingCycleEditedContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit show the contract's store credit setting.
  • Contract calculation: paymentConfiguration is a new optional input on SubscriptionContractCalculationContractCreateInput and SubscriptionContractCalculationContractUpdateInput. SubscriptionCalculatedContract.paymentConfiguration shows the value that the commit applies.
  • SubscriptionDraft: SubscriptionDraftInput.paymentConfiguration is available on subscriptionDraftUpdate, subscriptionContractCreate, and subscriptionContractAtomicCreate.

In the Customer Account API, SubscriptionContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit returns the store credit setting. Customer portals can display it, and the field is read-only.

The GraphQL Admin API applies the following validation rules:

title: RolloutChange now includes applyResult
summary:
As of GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01, the RolloutChange interface has an applyResult field. Applying a rollout makes a treatment's changes permanent for every buyer. applyResult shows the outcome of the latest attempt to apply each change, so your app can find changes that failed.

applyResult is null before the first attempt to apply the change. With an online access token, it's also null if the staff member can't read the changed resource. It uses the existing read_rollouts access scope.

query {
  rollout(id: "gid://shopify/Rollout/1") {
    treatments {
      changes(first: 10) {
        nodes {
          id
          applyResult {
            status
            completedAt
            errorCode
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

RolloutChangeApplyResult has three fields:

  • status: IN_PROGRESS, SUCCESS or FAILURE.
  • completedAt: when the attempt finished. It's null while in progress, or if the time wasn't recorded.
  • errorCode: why the change failed, when known: RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND, VALIDATION_FAILED, LIMIT_EXCEEDED, INVALID_CHANGE or INTERNAL_ERROR.

title: App Events: Send events from Admin UI extensions and embedded apps
summary:
Admin UI extensions and embedded apps can now send app events to Shopify with shopify.appEvents.emit(). At Editions, we launched app events for Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions. This release adds the Shopify admin, so you can now track app usage across all three surfaces. This is a new, optional API, so no action is required.

What changed

shopify.appEvents.emit() is now available on two more surfaces:

  • Admin UI extensions: Extensions that use API version 2027-01 or later can call shopify.appEvents.emit(). Extensions that you preview with shopify app dev can also send events.
  • Embedded apps (App Home): Apps that use App Bridge can call the same method from the app's pages in the Shopify admin.

The method takes an event handle and an optional object of attributes:

shopify.appEvents.emit("description_generated", {
  word_count: 120,
  placement: "product_details",
});

Shopify adds your app and the shop to each event, so you do not need an access token or a shop ID. Do not include data in attributes that could identify an individual, such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, staff member IDs, or customer IDs.

Events that Shopify accepts are visible in the Dev Dashboard logs, together with the events that your app backend sends. Events do not identify the extension that sent them or the staff member who used it.

Each Admin UI extension can send a burst of up to 20 events, then 2 events per second. An embedded app has the same limit, shared across the app in one Shopify admin tab. Events from Admin UI extensions and embedded apps are not processed for billing. To report usage for Shopify App Pricing, send a billing event from your app backend.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that have Admin UI extensions on API version 2027-01 or later, and to embedded apps that use App Bridge. Embedded apps do not need a specific API version. Admin UI extensions on earlier API versions do not have shopify.appEvents.

On should-render targets and data targets, emit() sends nothing and resolves {success: false, error: 'Emit is unavailable.'}. An embedded app gets the same result where the Shopify admin does not offer App Events.

What to do

No action is required as existing apps and extensions will continue to work without changes. If you want to send events from the Shopify admin, do these steps:

  1. For an Admin UI extension, set api_version = "2027-01" or later in shopify.extension.toml.
  2. Call shopify.appEvents.emit() with an event handle and optional attributes.
  3. Run shopify app dev and use the extension or app in a development store.
  4. Check the result of emit(). If success is false, read error for the cause.
  5. Open Logs in the Dev Dashboard to confirm that your events arrive.

Related docs

  • Send events from Admin UI extensions
  • Send events from embedded apps with App Bridge
  • Monitoring and logs in the Dev Dashboard

title: `draftOrderCreate` and `draftOrderUpdate` require the `apply_discounts_to_draft_orders` permission to add discounts
summary:
In all supported API versions, draftOrderCreate and draftOrderUpdate return a user error when an app acting as a staff member without the apply_discounts_to_draft_orders permission adds a discount to a draft order. The mutations don't save the draft order, return null for draftOrder, and return the refusal in userErrors.

What changed

When a request runs as a staff member who doesn't have the apply_discounts_to_draft_orders permission, draftOrderCreate and draftOrderUpdate reject any change that adds discounts through the DraftOrderInput:

  • Adding a discount code to discountCodes that the draft order doesn't already have.
  • Setting acceptAutomaticDiscounts to true on a draft order that doesn't already accept automatic discounts.

For draftOrderCreate, any non-empty discountCodes or acceptAutomaticDiscounts: true counts as adding a discount because the draft order doesn't exist yet.

In these cases, the mutation returns null for draftOrder and a user error on each field that adds a discount: discountCodes or acceptAutomaticDiscounts. For draftOrderUpdate, the field path starts with input. The mutation doesn't return a top-level GraphQL error.

Keeping or removing a draft order's existing discounts still works.

Example

This request adds a discount code and turns on automatic discounts for an existing draft order:

mutation draftOrderUpdate($id: ID!, $input: DraftOrderInput!) {
  draftOrderUpdate(id: $id, input: $input) {
    draftOrder {
      id
      discountCodes
      acceptAutomaticDiscounts
    }
    userErrors {
      field
      message
    }
  }
}

{
  "id": "gid://shopify/DraftOrder/276395349",
  "input": {
    "discountCodes": ["SUMMER10"],
    "acceptAutomaticDiscounts": true
  }
}

If the staff member doesn't have the apply_discounts_to_draft_orders permission, the response is:

{
  "data": {
    "draftOrderUpdate": {
      "draftOrder": null,
      "userErrors": [
        {
          "field": ["input", "discountCodes"],
          "message": "The user must have the apply_discounts_to_draft_orders permission to add a discount."
        },
        {
          "field": ["input", "acceptAutomaticDiscounts"],
          "message": "The user must have the apply_discounts_to_draft_orders permission to add a discount."
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

draftOrderCreate returns the same user errors, with the field paths ["discountCodes"] and ["acceptAutomaticDiscounts"] (no input prefix).

Who's affected

Apps that do all of the following are affected:

  • Calls draftOrderCreate or draftOrderUpdate as a staff member.
  • Expects to add discount codes or enable automatic discounts.
  • Doesn't ensure that the staff member has the apply_discounts_to_draft_orders permission.

Requests that don't act as a staff member, such as requests made with an offline access token, aren't affected.

What to do

  1. Check userErrors on draftOrderCreate and draftOrderUpdate for an error on discountCodes or acceptAutomaticDiscounts.
  2. If your app needs to add discounts, ask the merchant to give the staff member the Apply discounts permission under Draft orders.

  • Store permissions

title: Admin-created custom apps now appear in the Dev Dashboard
summary:
Custom apps created in the Shopify admin are moving to the Dev Dashboard, where you can view their logs and set up an IP allowlist. Existing integrations keep working.

What changed

Custom apps that merchants or staff created in the Shopify admin now appear in the Dev Dashboard. Manage existing admin-created custom apps in the Dev Dashboard, including credentials and logs.

Existing apps and integrations keep working:

  • Apps stay installed with their existing access scopes and webhook subscriptions.
  • Existing Admin API access tokens continue to work.

In the Dev Dashboard, these apps now have access to:

  • Configure IP restrictions to control which IP addresses can use the app’s credentials.
  • Inspect API and webhook logs to investigate unexpected activity and troubleshoot integration issues.

The migration doesn’t automatically replace any existing tokens or enable IP restrictions.

For more on building and managing apps in the Dev Dashboard, see the dev docs

Who’s affected

This change applies to custom apps that were created in the Shopify admin, including apps transferred to a merchant. These custom apps will now appear in the merchant’s Dev Dashboard.

Public apps and other app types that you already managed in the Dev Dashboard are not affected.

Why this matters

Managing all app types in the Dev Dashboard gives you:

  • Centralized control over app credentials and authentication.
  • IP restrictions that reduce the risk of credential misuse.
  • Logs for API calls and webhook deliveries that make it easier to audit traffic and debug issues.

This helps you secure existing integrations without breaking them and gives you better visibility into app behavior.

What to do

No immediate action is required for your apps to keep working. To improve security and observability, you should:

  1. Review each migrated custom app in the Dev Dashboard and confirm that it appears with the expected installation and scopes.
  2. Enable IP restrictions for each app where you can safely limit traffic to known IP addresses.
  3. Use the API and webhook logs in the Dev Dashboard to confirm that requests and deliveries look as expected after any changes.

After you enable IP restrictions, monitor the logs for a period of time to confirm that all integrations continue to function as expected.

title: Amazon EventBridge webhook payload size limit increased to 1 MB
summary:
You can now receive webhook and Events payloads up to 1 MB (1,000,000 bytes) through Amazon EventBridge, up from 256 KB. This increase applies automatically across all API versions, and you don't need to update your existing subscriptions.

What changed

Previously, Amazon EventBridge deliveries capped payloads at 256 KB:

  • Classic webhook payloads over 256 KB fell back to a minimal {"id": ...} body, requiring a follow-up Admin API request to fetch the full resource.
  • Events payloads over 256 KB used large-payload overflow and delivered a temporary payload_url download link instead of the inline payload.

Shopify now sends raw UTF-8 payloads up to 1,000,000 bytes directly to your Amazon EventBridge partner event source, leaving headroom under EventBridge's 1 MiB entry cap for the source, detail-type, and detail envelope. Large resources such as products with many variants or orders with many line items now arrive inline, reducing follow-up Admin API requests and payload_url downloads in your app.

Payloads over 1,000,000 bytes keep the existing fallback behavior: classic webhooks send {"id": ...}, and Events deliveries send a stub payload with payload_url, payload_size_bytes, and expires_at.

What to do

No action is required. Existing EventBridge subscriptions configured in shopify.app.toml or through the GraphQL Admin API (eventBridgeWebhookSubscriptionCreate and webhookSubscriptionCreate) automatically receive inline payloads up to 1 MB across all API versions.

To review how your app handles large deliveries:

  • Keep fallback handling in place for payloads that exceed 1 MB ({"id": ...} for classic webhooks and payload_url for Events), or narrow payloads with include_fields and targeted Events [events.subscription] query selections.
  • Verify that the downstream AWS targets attached to your EventBridge rules accept events up to 1 MB, or configure an EventBridge input transformer if a target enforces a smaller quota.

title: Updated B2B location access in the Customer Account API
summary:
We've changed what B2B customers can read on all versions of the Customer Account API. Customers now read only the company data and the orders for companies that they belong to.

Company location access

The schema doesn't change. Some fields now return null, an empty list, or fewer results.

CompanyContact.locations returns an empty list unless the contact belongs to the current customer. The current customer reads the locations that they have a role in from their contact's locations field, from Company.locations, and from companyLocation(id:).

On a CompanyLocation where the current customer has no role, the following fields return null or an empty list:

  • Tax field: taxIdentifier.
  • Contact fields: contacts and roleAssignments.

Orders after a customer is removed from a company

When a merchant removes a customer from a company, order(id:) and draftOrder(id:) refuse that company's orders and draft orders. customer.orders and customer.draftOrders exclude the orders and draft orders for that company. The customer's personal orders are still listed.

What you need to do

If your app reads a location's tax or contact data through another contact's locations or through an order's purchasingEntity, then expect null or an empty list for locations where the customer has no role. If your app shows a customer's order history, then the history omits the orders that the customer placed for a company that they no longer belong to. You don't need to change your queries.

title: Declare that your app uses only expiring Admin API tokens
summary:
Turn on the Admin API token expiry card from your app’s Settings page in the Dev Dashboard and any API requests made from your app to the GraphQL or REST Admin API must use expiring tokens. Requests made with non-expiring tokens will be rejected.

What changed

When you enable Admin API token expiry for an app, it applies across every store where that app is installed. GraphQL and REST Admin API requests then fail if they use either:

  • A non‑expiring offline access token
  • A delegate access token with more than 24 hours remaining before expiry

Enforcement can take up to 30 minutes to take effect. Enabling the setting doesn’t migrate or revoke existing tokens.

You can turn the setting off if you encounter issues. Turning it off doesn’t change the April 1, 2027 enforcement deadline for public apps or the December 1, 2026 requirement for custom apps.

Who’s affected

This setting is available for all app types in the Dev Dashboard. It affects an app only after you turn it on for that app.

Expiring tokens are required for all apps:

  • **December 1, 2026: ** Custom apps created on or after must use expiring tokens.
  • January 1, 2027: Public apps that still use non-expiring offline access tokens are delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working.
  • April 1, 2027: Shopify rejects a GraphQL Admin API or REST Admin API request that presents a non-expiring offline token, and merchants lose access to your app until they re-authenticate.

What to do

We recommend turning on Admin API token expiry to give you peace of mind that your migration is complete ahead of the deadlines.

  1. Complete your migration using the Admin API token expiry migration guide, then review your app’s GraphQL and REST logs for affected requests. The Dev Dashboard highlights potential token‑expiry issues detected in the last 14 days, though detection can lag by a day.
  2. Open your app in the Dev Dashboard, go to Settings, and select Turn on in the Admin API token expiry card. Confirm that you understand that requests that don’t meet token‑expiry requirements will fail.
  3. Allow up to 30 minutes for enforcement to take effect. Then check your app’s workflows and logs for rejected requests, including requests from background jobs, to confirm that your app handles expiring tokens correctly.

title: App security updates: Thank you, plus what's required next
summary:
Thanks to you, we've already seen the vast majority of apps that run bulk operations adopt an IP allowlist. That's a big step toward keeping merchants protected heading into the busiest weeks of the year.

Here's what's required, what's new, and what's coming next.

Action required

  • All public apps that call the Admin API: Turn on an IP allowlist by November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. Apps without one will be delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working. For apps that are delisted, we'll relist apps automatically once they add an IP allowlist. Set up your IP allowlist
  • Bulk operations: We're beginning enforcement on bulk queries and mutations from public apps without an IP allowlist. Turn on your allowlist to restore them.
  • Enable bulk operations for partner-created apps: Before your app can run bulk queries or bulk mutations, enable them from API access requests in the Partner Dashboard. If your app doesn't start a bulk query or mutation for 31 days, you'll need to enable it again. Read the changelog
  • Custom apps installed outside your organization also need an IP allowlist: These apps need an IP allowlist for new installs from November 20, 2026, and for existing installs from January 1, 2027. From January 1, one app without an allowlist blocks you from installing any of your apps on stores outside your organization. Apps installed only within your organization, and apps created by merchants, aren't affected. Read the changelog

New this week

  • You can now use IP addresses and ASNs together. Your allowlist can include IP addresses, CIDR ranges and your hosting provider's ASNs at the same time, with up to 250 IP addresses or ranges. A request is allowed if it matches any entry. Country restrictions apply only to ASNs. For the strongest protection, use specific IP addresses wherever you can. Read the changelog

Coming soon

  • MFA on every partner account. Starting next week, multi-factor authentication will be required on all partner accounts. We recommend passkeys. Turn on MFA now so it doesn't interrupt your work later. Protect the accounts that control your app

Get help

If you see something suspicious, tell us right away at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You're responsible for fixing it and notifying affected merchants, and we'll support you through it.

For general security questions, contact Shopify Support.

Everything lives in the App Security Hub, and we answer questions on the App Security board in the developer community.

title: Market metafields break ties between equally specific markets by market handle
summary: When a buyer matches two or more equally specific markets that set the same metafield, Market.metafield and Market.metafields now return the value from the market with the lowest handle, instead of the value that was updated most recently. This behavior change applies to the Storefront API, Liquid, and Function APIs on every API version. If your app or theme reads market metafields on stores with overlapping markets, check which value buyers get in a tie.

title: Market.metafields matches keys in any case as of Storefront API version 2027-01
summary:
As of Storefront API version 2027-01, the metafields field on the Market object matches each requested key in any case, as Market.metafield already does. This is a breaking change for apps and custom storefronts that request a market metafield key in a different case from the stored key, or that read a key that the buyer's markets store that differ by letter case. If your app does either, review its Market.metafields queries before you move it to 2027-01.

What changed

In version 2027-01, Market.metafields returns a metafield when the requested key matches the stored key in any case. In earlier versions, Market.metafields returns a metafield only when the requested key and the stored key have the same case.

For example, a market stores a metafield with the namespace custom and the key colour:

  • In version 2026-10 and earlier, the entry for { namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" } is null.
  • In version 2027-01, the entry returns the stored metafield.

Who's affected

The change applies to apps and custom storefronts that query metafields on a Market object, from Localization.market or Country.market, with Storefront API version 2027-01 or later. Your app is affected only if one of these conditions is true:

  • It requests a key in a different case from the key that the market stores.
  • The buyer's markets store the same key in different cases.

Your app isn't affected if it requests each key in the case that the markets store it, or if it uses only Market.metafield, which already matches keys in any case. Versions 2026-10 and earlier don't change.

Why this matters

In earlier versions, Market.metafield and Market.metafields can return different results for the same key: Market.metafield finds the metafield, and Market.metafields returns null. In 2027-01, both fields return the same metafield, so your storefront shows the same value whichever field it queries.

What to do

Market.metafield already matches keys case-insensitively, and it returns the metafield from the buyer's most specific market. So on the version that you use today, Market.metafield returns the result that Market.metafields returns in 2027-01. You can compare the two fields to find out whether the change affects your app.

  1. For each market metafield that your app reads, query Market.metafield and Market.metafields with the same namespace and key, and compare the results.
  2. If the results are the same for every key, then you don't need to make changes.
  3. If a result is different, then check whether the difference has a material impact on your app or your storefront.
  4. If it does, then update your app and your metafields so that they don't depend on the case of keys. For example, request each key in the case that your markets store it, and use one case for each key on every market.
query CompareMarketMetafields @inContext(country: CA) {
  localization {
    market {
      metafield(namespace: "custom", key: "Colour") {
        key
        value
      }
      metafields(identifiers: [{ namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" }]) {
        key
        value
      }
    }
  }
}
